stories.headline: Sharks premiership window nowhere near closing: Hynes
stories.summary: Cronulla halfback Nicho Hynes has refuted the widely held claim the Sharks' premiership window is about to close, as the club suffers from finals wobbles and prepares to farewell some big-name stars at season's end.
stories.body:
Cronulla halfback Nicho Hynes has refuted the widely held claim the Sharks' premiership window is about to close, as the club suffers from finals wobbles and prepares to farewell some big-name stars at season's end.

Since Hynes arrived at the Sharks from Storm in 2022, the club has played finals four years in a row but won only three of nine games, although they did the reach the preliminary final the last two seasons.

But at the end of 2026 they will bid goodbye to representative players Siona Katoa and centre Jesse Ramien (Cowboys), Siosifa Talakai (Perth Bears), Cameron McInnes (Super League) and Mawene Hiroti (Titans).

Balancing all that is crafty five-eighth Braydon Trindall, who returns early from a dislocated right shoulder for Saturday night's elimination final against North Queensland, has just turned 27, while rising stars like forwards Tom Hazelton, Jesse Colquhoun and damaging centre KL Iro have only played 60-odd NRL games.

"Whenever we're in this room preparing with the players we have at this club ... I'd be doing an injustice to this club and the players coming through if I said this was our only premiership window," Hynes said.

"It wouldn't be right by the younger players as that would be saying we didn't have belief in them.

"Whoever comes into this facility with a Sharks shirt on or a jersey is always going to do a great job because we've got the coaches and senior players here that make sure that standards are held.

"We've just got a good opportunity (this year) to try and win a premiership and hopefully we'll be doing that for many years to come."

First up is the Cowboys on Saturday night at Allianz Stadium with Trindall, whose nickname is 'Tricky', back in the No.6 jersey after three weeks out.

"Very keen ... it's been very tough sitting on the sidelines so very excited to be back."

Trindall spoke to the media with his shoulder heavily strapped and not knowing yet if postseason surgery is required.

"I just had to get the strength back to where it was, or near-abouts, before I did it," Trindall said.

"I've been working hard to get the mobility through it as well and it feels like it's 100%."

He knows the Cowboys forward pack headed by Jason Taumalolo, Griffin Neame, Heilum Luki and Reuben Cotter will be heading straight for the joint.

"Yep, I'm ready."

Hynes is also ready to reignite the halves partnership that was sporadic in 2022-24, but has been a regular feature for the Sharks the last two years.

"He brings more of a '7' role to the team if you will," Hynes said.

"I know I wear the No.7 -- we can both play that sort of role, but he's got an outstanding kicking game and can play on-ball a bit more which frees me up out the back to play my natural running game.

"That was our first run together out there today and it felt we were back on the bike again.

"When we're chiming in together on both sides of the field it just feels natural."

With a mediocre finals record of late, Hynes was asked which version of the Sharks needed to show up on Saturday.

"Just the best version, and all of you have seen some of the best version of the Sharks this year.

"If we bring that best version of the Sharks we're going to be hard to stop."

stories.headline: Predicting the 2026 NFL playoff field, plus Super Bowl pick
stories.summary: Which teams from last season's playoffs will return -- and which ones will miss out? Who will be the surprises in the bracket? And who will win the Super Bowl?
stories.body:
It's postseason projection time. With hours to go before the first game of the 2026 NFL season, I'm picking the 14 teams that will be celebrating after the league plays 272 regular-season games. There's so much football to come and so many unexpected things we'll see along the way, but like anyone else, I want to lay out the playoff field I expect to see in January before the games kick off in mid-September.

Of course, that would be too easy. If you've read this column over the past couple of years, you'll remember that there's a twist. One of the most common mistakes we make as football fans -- myself included -- is overconfidence in the teams we saw excel last year. We're collectively too inclined to pick teams that made the playoffs a year ago to make it back in the current season. Ask me to pick 2026 playoff teams without any constraints and I'd pick at least nine of the 14 teams that made it in 2025.

Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show'

History tells us that's underestimating the chaos and variance that comes with 17-game NFL seasons. The league has been using the 14-team playoff format for only a few years now, but if we go back to 2002 and treat the seventh-best team in each conference as a playoff team, about 56% of teams that make it to the postseason in any given season make it back the following year. That's just under eight teams per campaign.

Eight teams in, six teams out. There's no guarantee that 2026 will play out like an average season in terms of playoff returnees, but the evidence says our playoff predictions should start there. I'll take things a step further by looking at division champions and teams with losing records in 2025 to tailor the field even closer to what a historic playoff field typically looks like by the end of the regular season. I'll detail how those play out along the way. And at the end, I'll make my Super Bowl pick for the upcoming season.

Jump to a section:

2025 division champions

2025 wild-card berths

From out to in

Barnwell's Super Bowl pick

Which 2025 division champions will return to the playoffs?
Let's start by splitting last season's playoff teams into two groups. Since 2002, just under 60% of teams that won their division in a given year have made it back to the playoffs the following year. That's 4.8 teams per year, which we'll round up to five. So, of the eight division winners from 2025, I have to pick five to return to the playoffs in 2026.

We can split that even further. About 43% of division winners repeat as champs the following season, with teams such as the Tom Brady-era Patriots and the Patrick Mahomes-era Chiefs as near-perennial favorites to finish first. If we remove the Patriots and Chiefs from the data set, the rate of repeating divisional winners drops to 36%. That's an average of about three division winners retaining their titles each season.

One of the weirdest things about the 2025 season factors in here. In 2024, six of the eight teams that won their division the prior year retained their crowns, which was just the third time that has happened in the eight-division era. In 2025, everything went in the opposite direction. Just one of the eight reigning champs held on to its division title for another year. The one team that did so was the Philadelphia Eagles, who became the first team to win back-to-back titles in the NFC East in more than two decades. Four 2024 division champs -- the Chiefs, Ravens, Lions and Buccaneers -- missed the postseason outright in 2025.

History tells us to pick three division winners to repeat as champions, with two more making it back to the postseason as wild cards. I'll then be left with three division winners from 2025 that I'll need to pick to miss the playoffs entirely. I'm sure that won't upset anyone ...

Running through my options, I'm already beginning to squirm. I'm not sure there are three division winners with good chances of repeating in 2026. I like some of last season's wild-card teams more than the division winners. If this were just "pick eight playoff teams to repeat," I might have five division winners missing the playoffs. This is why I like doing this column in this very particular way -- it forces me to think about choices I don't necessarily love but that might turn out to be more realistic as the season plays out in the months to come.

Seattle Seahawks
My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (NFC West champions)

It feels almost controversial to pick the defending Super Bowl champions to stay atop the NFC West for another year. It's easy to understand why the Rams are favorites to top the Seahawks and return to the top of the division; they added Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald, Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson to their roster this offseason.

But the Seahawks did beat the Rams twice in three tries last season. They went 14-3, finishing two games ahead of Los Angeles in the race for the NFC West, and led the league in DVOA. Sure, the Seahawks were one of the league's healthier teams, especially on offense, but they also outscored opposing teams by more than 11 points per game and went a sustainable 4-3 in games decided by seven points or less.

The champs lost several players on defense (Coby Bryant, Riq Woolen and Boye Mafe among them), but coach Mike Macdonald has a significant track record of developing both young players and underappreciated veterans into useful contributors on the defensive side of the ball. And virtually everybody of note beyond Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III is back on offense. It would be a surprise if the Seahawks weren't competing for a division title this season.

Philadelphia Eagles
My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (NFC East champions)

If the Eagles were able to overcome what had been a multi-decade run of new champions in the NFC East to finally hold on to their division crown, I'm willing to back Jalen Hurts & Co. to make it three straight in 2026. Things didn't end well for the Eagles in 2025, as they lost four of their final seven games before being bounced out of the playoffs by the 49ers, but you might remember the Eagles going through a similar scenario in 2023. They started 10-1, lost five of their last six games and were then blown out by the Bucs in the wild-card round. Yet Philly won the division the following season -- and also won the Super Bowl.

The Eagles weren't great on offense, but things really began to crater once they lost star right tackle Lane Johnson in November. The 36-year-old is back as part of what should be a healthier offensive line. Vic Fangio fielded the youngest defense in the league last season, and that unit could be even more productive after adding Riq Woolen and Jonathan Greenard to the mix during the offseason. Sean Mannion's new under-center offensive scheme creates some uncertainty, but the Eagles have one of the highest floors of any team in the NFL.

New England Patriots
My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (AFC East champions)

I've already written about why I don't expect the Patriots to win 14 games again, which shouldn't be any sort of significant surprise. (It's hard to win 14 games twice in a row!) Even with a bit of a step backward, though, the Patriots could still hold on to their AFC East title with something like an 11-win campaign.

Their schedule is tougher, but it's still the 11th-easiest slate in the league per ESPN's Football Power Index. They'll probably suffer more injuries after being one of the healthiest teams a year ago, but unless stars such as Drake Maye, Christian Gonzalez and A.J. Brown miss significant time, the Patriots should still have plenty of talent. And if the blitz-happy defensive scheme that helped sustain the Patriots as their offense struggled during the AFC playoffs carries over into 2026, the Pats might actually be a better team on a snap-by-snap basis than they were in 2025 -- even if that doesn't produce a similar win-loss record as a product of playing stiffer competition.

Denver Broncos
My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (AFC wild card)

Likewise, although I expect the Broncos to decline after a banner 2025 campaign, there's still plenty of room for them to do so and still make it back to the postseason for the third consecutive year. Denver won the AFC West by three games last season. The team's 24-10 record since the start of 2024 is tied for the third best in the NFL, one game behind the Bills and Eagles.

The Broncos were very healthy last season, but it's notable that they were able to overcome a 3½-game stretch without Pat Surtain II, winning all four of those games. And while Bo Nix still had issues with consistency and accuracy, he jumped from 18th in Total QBR over the first half of the season to 11th over the remainder of the regular season and postseason. If coach Sean Payton can coax out the version of Nix we saw outduel Josh Allen in a playoff shootout more often in 2026, could the Broncos be the most complete team in football?

Pittsburgh Steelers
My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (AFC wild card)

We'll see just how thoroughly the Steelers are impacted by the departure of Mike Tomlin. Mike McCarthy should offer an offensive coaching upgrade for a team that hasn't really ever replaced Bruce Arians. McCarthy isn't exactly the analytics wizard that his initial news conferences in Dallas suggested, but the Steelers were way behind the curve in terms of game management by the time Tomlin finished his run in Pittsburgh. A more modern approach might help the Steelers squeeze more out of their roster.

I'm not optimistic about Aaron Rodgers making a deep playoff run in what is expected to be his final year as a pro, but the Steelers don't have many other weaknesses to their roster. They're one of the league's most underrated teams in the trenches, with a young, promising offensive line led by Zach Frazier and Troy Fautanu. There's a great pass rush and what could potentially be an excellent secondary if Joey Porter Jr. is on the field. Facing the league's eighth-easiest schedule, the Steelers should be able to approach 10 wins and get back into the postseason, even without Tomlin in the picture.

Carolina Panthers
My pick for 2026: Out of the playoffs

Somebody had to win the NFC South last season. While the Panthers picked up impressive wins over the Packers and Rams during the regular season, they ranked either third or fourth in the division by most advanced metrics. They finished 25th in DVOA and won a three-way tiebreaker with the Buccaneers and Falcons at 8-9.

I'm not sure any of the teams in the NFC South are good enough to separate from the pack, but after finishing first a year ago, the Panthers are facing the toughest schedule of any team in their division this season. They've also already been battered by injuries, with players such as Taylor Moton, Tershawn Wharton, Nic Scourton, Ikem Ekwonu and Chris Brazzell II already out before the regular season begins. It's tough to feel really confident in Carolina at the moment, although it's admittedly hard to feel that way about any of its divisional brethren, either.

Jacksonville Jaguars
My pick for 2026: Out of the playoffs

The Jags rode a massive increase in defensive takeaways and a second half full of games against second- and third-string quarterbacks to make a nine-game leap and jump into the postseason. There are talented players on defense, and Travis Hunter could help shore up what had been a weak spot at corner if he's there on something close to a full-time basis in 2026. But the playoff push was really driven by a defense that ranked sixth in DVOA, and the Jaguars won't be as healthy or force as many turnovers this season.

Most of the discussion around the Jags surrounds the offense, and while Trevor Lawrence ended the regular season protecting the football, the unit finished only 14th in DVOA. There's a scenario where the offense is much better in 2026, but it involves a lot of counting on the best versions of players such as Brian Thomas Jr., Bhayshul Tuten, Cole Van Lanen and Parker Washington all showing up at the same time. I have serious reservations about the running game and the offensive line, and playing a league-high 11 games away from their home stadium won't help matters. This could be a consolidation year for Jacksonville.

Chicago Bears
My pick for 2026: Out of the playoffs

It could also be one for the Bears, who made major strides under Ben Johnson in the young coach's first year at the helm, especially on offense. We saw a team that relied almost entirely on fourth-quarter success on offense, takeaways on defense and a series of perfectly timed meltdowns by its opposition to win a bunch of close games. And history tells us that's just not a sustainable way to win games year after year.

Caleb Williams could go supernova this season and compete for an MVP award, and the 2026 Bears could play at a much higher level for all four quarters of games on offense. An overhauled defense could play much better on a snap-by-snap basis, too. That scenario absolutely exists. The numbers suggest that the Bears are going to take a step backward before moving forward, though, and in a division where every team posted a winning record in 2025, that might be enough to drop Chicago out of the postseason.

Which 2025 wild-card teams will return to the playoffs?
Here's where this gets really painful. I'd argue that the six teams that claimed wild-card berths last season collectively have a better shot of winning the Super Bowl in 2026 than the eight reigning divisional champs. While the five teams I projected as most likely to decline this upcoming season were all 2025 divisional champions, there are no obvious regression candidates here.

But history tells us that just under 54% of wild-card teams since 2002 make it back to the postseason the following year. (That number includes seventh seeds as postseason qualifiers even before the league expanded to the 14-team playoff.) As a result, to abide by what we should expect from a typical year, I have to pick three of last season's wild-card teams to make it into the playoffs and three to miss out. Gulp.

Los Angeles Rams
My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (NFC wild card)

Well, one of the picks to make the postseason was easy. The Rams were the widespread Super Bowl favorites even before Aaron Donald unretired, adding an almost comical level of star power and depth to what was already the league's scariest defensive line. ESPN's FPI gives the Rams a better chance of winning the Super Bowl (17%) than missing the playoffs outright (16%).

The Chiefs missing the playoffs last year despite having a healthy Patrick Mahomes until mid-December is a reminder that no team is guaranteed a trip to the postseason in any given year. At the same time, it's difficult to put together a scenario where the Rams miss the playoffs. Even if Matthew Stafford does get hurt or takes a major step backward at 38, the Rams could turn to first-round pick Ty Simpson, who would be supported by some of the league's best playmakers, arguably its best offensive architect and a defense overloaded with talent.

And heck, if Sean McVay coaxed Donald out of retirement, what's stopping him from adding another future Hall of Famer or two between now and January?

Houston Texans
My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (AFC South champions)

The 2025 Texans became just the second team since 2002 to start 0-3 and still advance to the postseason, following in the footsteps of the 2018 Texans. And after that 0-3 start, they were as good as any team in football. Despite losing C.J. Stroud for a month, the Texans went 12-2, outscored their opponents by nearly nine points per game and led all defenses in points allowed per drive (1.5).

Stroud melted down in the postseason, which is obviously a concern if it carries over into 2026, but he was better in the regular season than those playoff memories would suggest. He has been a solid-or-better starter without any semblance of a running game, and if the move to add David Montgomery behind a reconfigured offensive line finally unlocks the Texans on the ground, we could see something closer to the rookie-year version of Stroud this season. The combination of Stroud, a truly dominant defense and a relatively weak division gives Houston a high floor.

Buffalo Bills
My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (AFC wild card)

Speaking of teams with high floors, Josh Allen's streak of 137 consecutive starts gives the Bills a massive advantage on just about every other team in the league. Buffalo's 83-33 record since 2019 puts it one game behind the Chiefs, with the Bills rolling off seven consecutive seasons with double-digit victories over that span. They're the only team in the NFL to make it to the playoffs in each of the past seven years.

This is a transitional year for them. The Bills are moving to a new stadium without fired head coach Sean McDermott, who had been in charge since 2017. That creates some uncertainty. Will Joe Brady be an effective head coach? Will the offense suffer as Brady's focus spreads to the entire team? I'm optimistic about debuting defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard after seeing what he did at Wisconsin, but the Bills have major question marks in the secondary.

If Leonhard can transform the defense, Buffalo could be the best team in the league. If there are growing pains on both sides of the ball, the Bills should still be a playoff team -- but they might not be able to usurp the Patriots and reclaim the AFC East.

San Francisco 49ers
My pick for 2026: Out of the playoffs

The 49ers don't really do middle of the pack. Under Kyle Shanahan, they have four seasons with 12 or more wins, but they also have four with six wins or fewer. Those subpar years are usually a product of injuries, an issue that seems to perpetually plague the Niners. They've had only one even vaguely healthy season in recent years, which came in 2023. Naturally, that was the year the 49ers made it to the Super Bowl, where in-game injuries to Jon Feliciano and Dre Greenlaw might have decided a close contest with the Chiefs.

Well, as we enter Week 1, the 49ers are already banged up. Ricky Pearsall is already out for the year. Offseason additions Nate Hobbs and Christian Kirk are on injured reserve, while 2025 first-round pick Mykel Williams is on the physically unable to perform list. Veteran fullback Kyle Juszczyk, big free agent signing Mike Evans, starting corner Renardo Green and second-round pick De'Zhaun Stribling (who was one of the breakout stars in training camp) have all missed practice time with injuries. And of course, Shanahan himself was shaken up after a scary automobile accident before camp began.

The good news has Nick Bosa and George Kittle traveling to Australia to play in the season opener, but both veterans are coming off serious injuries and might not be 100% to start the season. Fred Warner is returning from a badly fractured ankle. And so many of the other key players on San Francisco's roster -- including Trent Williams, Christian McCaffrey, Greenlaw and even starting quarterback Brock Purdy -- have long track records of struggling to stay healthy for full seasons.

A healthy 49ers team would be one of the best in football, but that's always a difficult ask. And after going 5-1 in one-score games last season, San Francisco can't count on pulling out so many close ones in 2026.

Los Angeles Chargers
My pick for 2026: Out of the playoffs

It's no fun picking against the Chargers, who perpetually have a Super Bowl ceiling given the core of star talent on their roster at key positions. And like everyone else, I'm extremely excited to see what new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel can do with Justin Herbert, two high-end tackles in Joe Alt and Rashawn Slater, and a group of promising young playmakers led by Omarion Hampton and Ladd McConkey. There's a chance that the Chargers combine what has been one of the league's best defenses with a resurgent offense and look like the very best team in the NFL this year.

There's also a scenario where things don't go quite as well. The defense lost star coordinator Jesse Minter, who joined the Ravens to take over as their new head coach. New coordinator Chris O'Leary will be in that role for the first time at any level. Minter was able to coax improved play from veterans Donte Jackson and Khalil Mack while developing youngsters such as Cam Hart, Tarheeb Still and Daiyan Henley into immediate contributors. It wouldn't be a surprise if the defense took a step backward this season.

And while Herbert will undoubtedly be excited about getting his two standout tackles back in the lineup, the interior of the O-line looms as a potential weakness, especially after Tyler Biadasz tore an ACL this summer. Second-round pick Jake Slaughter will step in at center, but the duo of Kayode Awosika and Cole Strange has much to prove at guard if McDaniel wants to install the sort of run game he was known for in Miami. The Chargers will also face what projects to be the league's seventh-toughest schedule, while their division rivals in Kansas City and Denver land at 17th and 18th, respectively.

Green Bay Packers
My pick for 2026: Out of the playoffs

After picking the Packers to win the NFC and make it to the Super Bowl each of the past two years, I'm reluctantly forced by the structure of this column to bow out and hop off their bandwagon this year. I'm still a believer in the core talent on this roster, and with so many players who are either entering or in the middle of their prime, Matt LaFleur should have some of his young contributors break out and hit a new level in 2026. Jordan Love, who has led the NFL in Total QBR since the second half of the 2023 season, is already one of the league's most underappreciated quarterbacks.

In 2026, though, this roster has a lot of questions. Micah Parsons will start the year on the physically unable to perform list, and it's unclear when the Packers can count on him to look like his usual self as he recovers from a torn ACL. The Packers traded away Rashan Gary this offseason for cap relief after the Parsons deal, meaning that their lead returning pass rusher in terms of sack production to start the season is Devonte Wyatt, who had four in 2025. The Packers didn't have a first-round pick to help supplement the defense this offseason, and defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley left to take over as the head coach in Miami.

The offense is also in flux. Rasheed Walker and Elgton Jenkins both left during the offseason, leaving former first-round pick Jordan Morgan -- who hasn't looked great at guard -- to move to left tackle. The five backup linemen on the roster have a combined 76 career snaps on offense. Luke Musgrave is out indefinitely with a neck injury, which could limit Green Bay's ability to play out of multi-tight end sets, even with the return of Tucker Kraft. And lead back Josh Jacobs was placed on the commissioner exempt list last week, leaving the Packers to turn their run game over to three young backs, none of whom has ever carried the ball more than 40 times in a single season.

It already feels like the Packers are hanging on for dear life, and the season hasn't even begun.

Which teams will go 'outhouse to penthouse' in 2026?
With the 49ers, Bears, Chargers, Jaguars, Packers and Panthers all missing the playoffs in this scenario, I need to pick six teams that missed out last season to take their places. And naturally, the right place for me to start is ... at the bottom. Since 2002, about 31% of teams that finished in the bottom five of their respective conferences in a given year have finished as a top-seven seed the following season.

So, taking the 10 worst teams in the NFL -- five from each conference -- a year ago, I need to pick three of them to massively improve and make it to the postseason in 2026. This is where I had the most success last year. I picked the Bears (coming off a 5-12 season), Jaguars (4-13) and 49ers (6-11) to make it to the playoffs, and all three got there. Of course, I also picked the Cardinals as one of the other new postseason teams, and they finished dead last in the NFC, so I won't be patting myself too hard on the back.

Kansas City Chiefs
My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (AFC West champions)

This one won't be quite as controversial as picking the Bears or Jaguars last year, of course. I laid out the case for the Chiefs in my column on teams likeliest to improve last month, built around their record in one-score games bouncing back after falling from 10-0 in 2024 to 1-9 in 2025, the biggest single-season swing in history.

It's too simplistic to say that the difference will be getting back Patrick Mahomes, given that Mahomes went 6-8 as the starter a year ago, but the Chiefs were a pretty good team by advanced metrics with their future Hall of Famer on the field. They ranked ahead of the Broncos in DVOA as late as Week 14, which was Mahomes' last full game before the ACL tear. The 2024 Chiefs were an above-average team with spectacular luck. The 2025 team was an above-average team with truly awful luck. The 2026 edition expects to land somewhere in the middle, which should place Kansas City in the range of 11 or 12 wins.

Dallas Cowboys
My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (NFC wild card)

The Cowboys also project to improve in 2026 after making massive upgrades on defense. As Nick Harris of the Fort Worth Star-Telegram noted, 17 of the 26 defensive players who were on Dallas' roster in Week 1 last September aren't on NFL rosters right now. In addition to new defensive coordinator Christian Parker, the Cowboys could have as many as seven new starters on the field to begin the year on Sunday against the Giants.

Those defenders should also be luckier. The Cowboys forced takeaways on only 6.2% of opposing drives last season, which ranked 30th in the league, ahead of only the Commanders and Jets. Their 1.1% interception rate was also third worst in the league, ahead of the 49ers and Jets, who famously did not intercept a single pass all season. The Cowboys have lost star guard Tyler Smith to a thumb injury for the first month, but they're returning all 11 starters from what was one of the league's best offenses in 2025. If the defense can just be adequate, the Cowboys should be able to make it back to the postseason.

New York Giants
My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (NFC wild card)

The Giants? Yes, the same Giants who finished 4-13 in 2025. Do I think they're better than the Packers? No. But acknowledging that history tells us three teams from this bucket at the bottom of the 2025 standings will make it to the playoffs in 2026, the Giants look a lot like the Bears and Jaguars did a year ago -- better than it seemed the year before and in position to make a leap.

The Giants went 1-6 in one-score games, losing three contests in which they held a lead in the final minute of regulation and four in which their win probability topped 90% in the fourth quarter. That can be a product of a team that doesn't know how to win, but as we saw with the shift between the 2024 and 2025 Bears and what they did in the fourth quarters of games, even young teams tend to figure out that side of the game quicker than expected.

Injuries tormented key players for the Giants last season, but it appears Jaxson Dart, Malik Nabers and Andrew Thomas will all be on the field in Week 1, something we saw for only a handful of snaps last year. One of the league's deepest pass rushes should be capable of tormenting opposing pass protection units, but there are real questions about the run defense, which was a mess even before trading defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II.

The most important upgrade might be head coach John Harbaugh, who joins after an 18-year run with the Ravens. His experience and game management skills should help the Giants in those close games, but it's fair to note that Giants fans aren't especially enthused about his staff, particularly the decision to hire Matt Nagy and Greg Roman to run the offense. Of course, you could also make the case that they've both overseen playoff offenses in multiple stops around the league.

Can New York overcome a difficult schedule? The Giants rank eighth in projected strength of schedule, per the FPI, with a slightly easier slate than the Cowboys and Commanders, whom they might compete with for a playoff spot. Of course, a year ago, the Bears were projected to face the league's fourth-toughest schedule heading into the season, but with improved coaching and a step forward from their second-year quarterback, they jumped from worst to first in the NFC North. I don't think the Giants make that sort of push and win the division, but I do think they're capable of being the league's most surprising wild-card team.

Which teams will fill the final three playoff spots?
That leaves us with three remaining playoff spots for newcomers. And as you might have noticed, we're still looking for three division champions. That means we'll be solely picking teams from the NFC South, AFC North and NFC North to finish up.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers
My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (NFC South champions)

I'm not sure any of the four teams in the NFC South should be huge favorites, but somebody has to win it. I'll lean toward the Buccaneers, who saw their run game deteriorate last season as they battled injuries to both their lead back (Bucky Irving) and much of their offensive line. Baker Mayfield was able to pull out games with fourth-quarter magic early in the season, but the offense stagnated as the year went along. Tampa also had some of the worst special teams in the league, which should hopefully be alleviated by the addition of legendary Steelers special teams coach Danny Smith.

While the Bucs shed talent in losing veteran standouts Mike Evans and Jamel Dean this offseason, they were able to retain Vita Vea and should be the best team in the division along the offensive and defensive lines. Mayfield, having finally agreed to terms Tuesday on the long-term contract he sought, should still have enough in the way of playmaking talent to live up to the new deal.

And in reality, this might be more about process of elimination than anything else. I've already laid out my concerns about an injury-hit Panthers team. The Saints were two games off the pace in 2025 and were carried to six wins by a defense that has lost three key players in Demario Davis, Alontae Taylor and Bryan Bresee. And the Falcons don't appear to have a solution they feel good about at quarterback, while their 2025 first-round picks on the edge are either out for the year (Jalon Walker) or suspended for half the season (James Pearce Jr.). I don't feel great about the Bucs, but I feel worse about everyone else.

Baltimore Ravens
My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (AFC North champions)

The Ravens aren't exactly a sleeper pick to return to the postseason, given that they have the second-highest playoff chances in the league, per the FPI, as we approach the start of the year. Their case is simple: a healthier year from Lamar Jackson and a more consistently productive season from the defense under new head coach Jesse Minter, who did wonders in Los Angeles with the Chargers. Zach Orr's defense ranked 17th in DVOA last season while ranking as the league's third-most injured unit by adjusted games lost, and the Ravens will hope to line up star defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike next to new addition Trey Hendrickson up front for most of 2026.

Can you pick holes in that logic? Sure. Madubuike might not be his usual self after recovering from a serious neck injury. The Ravens look thin in the secondary and are relying on veteran corners Marlon Humphrey and Chidobe Awuzie to stay healthy. The interior of the offensive line was rebuilt and will take time to jell. And new offensive coordinator Declan Doyle -- less than a year older than Jackson -- will be overseeing an evolved version of what had been one of the league's best offenses under Todd Monken. I'm still picking the Ravens to win the division, but there are real questions Baltimore has to answer if it wants to make a deep playoff run in January.

Detroit Lions
My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (NFC North champions)

My final playoff spot came down to a battle between the Lions and Vikings in the NFC North. There are reasons to be optimistic about both teams, of course. Detroit was within one half of making the Super Bowl in 2023 and was the top seed in the conference in 2024 before some bad luck cost it a playoff spot in 2025. And as Kevin O'Connell has pointed out, the Vikings have put together 13- and 14-win seasons over the past five years when they've been able to piece together even competent quarterback play from the likes of Kirk Cousins and Sam Darnold -- a level Kyler Murray should hopefully be able to match in 2026.

I wouldn't be surprised if both teams made it to the postseason in 2026, but under the constraints of this system, I can pick only one. I leaned toward the Lions for a few reasons. One is schedule. Detroit projects to play the league's second-easiest slate of opponents in 2026, per the FPI. The Vikings, surprisingly, come up with the league's 17th-easiest schedule, even though they share many similar opponents. Both teams will face the AFC East and NFC South this year, but the Lions get the Cardinals, Giants and Titans as additionals, whereas the Vikings have the 49ers, Commanders and Colts. The FPI also sees the Lions as a more difficult opponent for the Vikings than vice versa.

The Lions should, at least in theory, be healthier on defense than they were in 2024 and 2025, when they ranked last in adjusted games lost in back-to-back campaigns. Admittedly, that starts with Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph opening the year on the physically unable to perform list, so things aren't off to a great start, but the rest of the defense is healthier than it was a year ago. The Vikings, meanwhile, should be more banged-up by the end of 2026 after ranking fifth and fourth in AGL over the prior two seasons, respectively, even if they're healthier than the Lions to open the season.

And of course, while the Vikings should have an advantage in terms of defensive performance, the Lions do project to be much better on the other side of the ball, where they have best-offense-in-football upside. While acknowledging that they've cycled through quarterbacks, the Vikings are yet to even land in the top 10 in a single season for offensive EPA per play under O'Connell, ranking 12th, 15th, 15th again and 28th over the past four seasons. We just don't know if Murray will be a good fit for O'Connell's offense or if the Vikings can keep him healthy for the entire season, something the new starter has managed only once in the past five years.

The Vikings also relied heavily on veterans last season, fielding the league's third-oldest team, including its second-oldest defense. Minnesota will be younger along the interior of the line this year, but it is still relying on several veterans in key spots, including newly re-signed safety Harrison Smith, who will be 37 this season. If those guys stay healthy and play well, all is good. If not, well, the Vikings don't possess a very deep roster. That might represent the difference as both these teams get through a 17-game season.

And ... who will win the Super Bowl?
Well, I naturally have to throw in a Super Bowl pick here. I've predicted Chiefs-Packers in the Super Bowl each of the past two years as part of a six-year stretch of choosing the Chiefs as eventual champs. Obviously, there have been years where that has gone really well, but that wasn't the case a year ago. The Chiefs missed the playoffs outright, and after injuries to Jordan Love and Micah Parsons, the Packers were only the seventh seed (and lost to the Bears in the wild-card round). I've already picked the Packers to miss the postseason earlier in this column, so I won't get to them here.

On the NFC side, I'll pick the Eagles. I really believe in their defense as potentially being the league's most complete unit, with difference-makers at all three levels and one of the best defensive coaches in Vic Fangio. There's understandable skepticism about the offense after the Eagles made coaching changes and moved on from legendary offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland, but when Lane Johnson has been on the field, the Eagles have been successful. The star right tackle should be in the lineup more often in 2026, and the Eagles will have more success running the ball than they did a year ago. They're one of the few teams that can compete with the Rams along the line of scrimmage and hold up in coverage against their playmakers.

And then in the AFC, with no clear favorite, I'm willing to make a leap of faith and continue backing the Chiefs. I'm cautiously optimistic about Mahomes given that he'll be on the field Week 1, and Andy Reid's team should have a more complete roster than what it lined up in 2025 after signing Kenneth Walker III and making significant investments along the defensive line. The offensive line should be healthier, although getting Josh Simmons on the field early in the season would be important. The schedule is easier earlier in the year, which should help a Chiefs team trying to evolve its identity after an offseason full of changes. The Bills and Ravens should still be dangerous if the coaching changes unlock their defenses, but I'm willing to believe in at least one more run from the Mahomes-Travis Kelce-Chris Jones core.

That leaves us with a Super Bowl rubber match. And as you can probably guess, if I believed enough in the Chiefs to pick them to win the AFC, I'll ride with them to gain a measure of revenge and beat the Eagles in Super Bowl LXI. The added rushing element with Walker will give the Eagles issues they didn't face when these two teams met in Super Bowl LIX, when the Chiefs basically abandoned the run altogether after the Eagles took an early lead.

Without the ability to pin their ears back and strictly go after Mahomes as a passer, the Eagles might not be quite as dominant on defense this time around. Jalen Hurts has been spectacular in the Super Bowl matchups against Mahomes, but his one fumble in Super Bowl LVII helped swing seven points back to the Chiefs in a 38-35 victory. This one wouldn't be quite as high-scoring, but let's say that the Chiefs let Kelce (and potentially other members of the organization) ride off into the sunset.

My pick: Chiefs 27, Eagles 24

stories.headline: George Russell follows Lando Norris in getting Silverstone grandstand
stories.summary: George Russell has got his wish after his grandstand joust with Lando Norris at Silverstone.
stories.body:
George Russell has got his wish after his grandstand joust with Lando Norris at Silverstone.

The Mercedes man has followed in his McLaren rival's footsteps as Silverstone announced the George Russell Grandstand would be opened at the circuit's Farm Curve for next year's race.

Norris debuted his 'Landostand' in 2025 when he claimed his maiden British Grand Prix win and this year 16,000 fans packed it out at Stowe corner.

Russell revealed his desire to also have a grandstand for his own race and quipped during this year's Silverstone weekend that he quite fancied taking some of Norris' seats.

"Good luck," Norris retorted. "I have more passionate fans and a better fanbase I think. Mine was more wanted from a public point of view, which is a great thing.

"He can do what he wants, but he is certainly not taking any of my seats."

Russell has now got his own spot at the famous circuit, with Mercedes posting pictures of their driver throughout his karting and junior racing career with the captain: "This is the kid that just got his own grandstand."

Russell said: "We are on the exit of turn one, you can see all of turn one and turn two, overtaking spot into three and turn four. It is a really, really cool place on the circuit -- one of the best in my opinion."

stories.summary: The Pelicans have traded Jordan Hawkins, Micah Peavy, a future second-round draft pick and a future second-round pick swap to the Grizzlies for AJ Johnson and Taj Gibson.
stories.body:
The New Orleans Pelicans have traded Jordan Hawkins, Micah Peavy, a future second-round draft pick and a future second-round pick swap to the Memphis Grizzlies for AJ Johnson and Taj Gibson.

The trade, which was announced Tuesday, clears roster space for the Pelicans, frees up salary flexibility to sign Bennedict Mathurin to a two-year, $16 million deal, and allows New Orleans to have a look at a young player in the 21-year-old Johnson, who was the No. 21 pick in the 2024 draft.

Hawkins, a lottery pick at No. 14 in the 2023 draft, now gets dealt by his team prior to his fourth season.

The Grizzlies, who picked up draft assets in the deal, will have multiple roster decisions before the start of the season as they are several guaranteed contracts above the 15 maximum.

Hawkins, 24, averaged 5.1 points in 51 games last season and struggled to find consistent playing time in New Orleans' crowded backcourt rotation. The former UConn star played just 13.6 minutes per game, a significant decrease from the 2024-25 season, when he played 23.6 minutes per game and averaged 10.8 points per game.

The Pelicans will be the fifth team in three seasons for the 6-foot-5 Johnson, who split last season between the Washington Wizards and Dallas Mavericks.

The Mavericks traded Johnson to the Grizzlies for Santi Aldama in July, five months after Johnson was included in the Anthony Davis blockbuster trade between Dallas and Washington. Johnson was drafted by the Milwaukee Bucks in 2024 before being traded later that season to the Wizards.

The trade saves New Orleans $5.7 million in salary, according to ESPN's Bobby Marks. Johnson was not allowed to be aggregated in a deal until Tuesday -- two months from the Aldama trade.

Gibson, 41, appeared in 10 games with Memphis last season. The 17-year veteran has played for eight different teams in his NBA career.

The 6-foot-7 Peavy appeared in 61 games as a rookie last season for the Pelicans, averaging 4.3 points.

stories.headline: Potential WNBA commissioner candidates to succeed Cathy Engelbert
stories.summary: Executives from the WNBA, NBA and Nike are among potential candidates to succeed Cathy Engelbert when she retires.
stories.body:
The WNBA is in search of a new leader, as commissioner Cathy Engelbert announced Friday that she will retire at the end of the calendar year.

Engelbert is the sixth league head and second-longest tenured behind Val Ackerman. Engelbert is the first to hold the title of WNBA commissioner, as the previous leaders served as president.

The process to find Engelbert's replacement will start later this month, if not sooner, sources told ESPN. Presumably, the hire will be made by and report to NBA commissioner Adam Silver, as was the case with Engelbert. She told the Associated Press and The IX that she has been working on a succession plan for years, and that she has already submitted a list of potential internal and external candidates to Silver.

It is unclear who else might have input on the decision, though the Board of Governors is expected to be involved. Prior to hiring Engelbert in 2019, the players' union also requested and was granted the opportunity to meet with the league's final candidates.

A source familiar with the situation told ESPN that the league is approaching the process with an open mind -- recognizing that the WNBA is now at a point where a leader without a traditional background in the corporate world might offer advantages.

Building and managing relationships with players, as well as owners, executives and business leaders, is also seen as a priority following Engelbert's tenure, which notably included several strained relationships with key players

Since Engelbert's announcement Friday, people around the league have speculated about who might be part of the candidate pool. Here are some of the names ESPN has heard as possibilities.

Swin Cash

The former UConn star played in the WNBA from 2002 to 2016, winning three championships. Inducted into the Naismith Hall of Fame in 2022, Cash has worked in the front office for the WNBA's New York Liberty (2017-19) and NBA's New Orleans Pelicans (2019-25). Cash, who turns 47 later this month, has also been a broadcast analyst. Her management experience is a plus, but some might question if Cash has spent enough time in the business world. -- Michael Voepel

Keia Clarke

She has been with the New York Liberty since 2011 and was promoted to CEO in 2020. She manages all business aspects of the franchise. Clarke played collegiate basketball at Canisius from 1999 to 2003 and began her career working for the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame. Clarke, 45, then went to work for the WNBA/NBA league offices before joining the Liberty. She has postgraduate business degrees from NYU and Harvard. Clarke knows the ins and outs of a WNBA franchise business and has been part of the huge growth of the Liberty in the past seven years. -- Voepel

Bethany Donaphin

Currently head of WNBA operations, Donaphin has been with the league since 2016. She played at Stanford from 1998 to 2002, then competed professionally in the WNBA and overseas from 2002 to 2008. She earned an MBA in 2012 from Pennsylvania's Wharton School and then spent 2013 to 2016 at Deloitte, consulting for Fortune 500 companies. Donaphin, 46, has worked with former WNBA president Lisa Borders and Engelbert at the WNBA. One of the questions regarding Donaphis is whether her close ties to Engelbert during the past seven years would be seen as a negative by the players, considering their criticisms of Engelbert. -- Voepel

Tanya Hvizdak

A vice president of global sports marketing at Nike, Hvizdak has spent 25 years at the company. Nike is the outfitter for the WNBA and NBA, agreeing to a 12-year extension for that role in 2024. Hvizdak has been closely involved in the development and rollout of shoes for prominent WNBA athletes such as A'ja Wilson, Caitlin Clark and Sabrina Ionescu. Hvizdak also spearheaded a Nike think tank, which included Serena Williams and Ionescu, in 2022 that focused on issues faced by female athletes. Hvizdak played collegiate basketball, first at Rhode Island and then Bentley, where she earned an MBA. Hvizdak has worked hard to elevate women's athletics and has extensive marketing and business knowledge. Would she want to relocate across the country from Portland to New York and take on a different type of role running the WNBA? -- Voepel

Nneka Ogwumike

If one of Engelbert's weaknesses was developing relationships with players, that's Ogwumike's clear strength. The Stanford grad is well-respected as WNBPA president for 10 years, a tenure that includes representing the players for two CBA negotiations. If Ogwumike is interested in the role, it would be a fascinating and unprecedented turn coming less than a year removed from a contentious labor negotiation between the players' union and the league/owners; Ogwumike has built a legacy representing the former, but the commissioner's job is to represent the latter.

Ogwumike, who recently announced she'll be retiring from the WNBA at the end of the season, has been asked if she would be interested in being WNBA commissioner. She responded, "I don't close doors, but I do appreciate vacation. There is so much that I don't know, and there is so much that I would have to learn before even, if an opportunity like that were to come for me, to be ready for that." So perhaps it's more realistic that Ogwumike would seek some other experiences first before pursuing that sort of leadership role. Either way, the league could gauge her interest in taking a sort of liaison role where she'd serve as a bridge between the league office and teams/players. -- Philippou

Jess Smith

In a similar vein to Clarke, Smith would be someone coming from the business side of a WNBA franchise. She has been at the helm as team president of the massively successful Golden State Valkyries since 2024. On the court, the Valkyries surpassed expectations by becoming the league's first expansion team to make the playoffs in its inaugural season. According to CNBC, the Valkyries are the first women's sports team with a $1 billion valuation. Smith has two decades of experience in pro sports, with previous stops at the team level in the MLB, NHL, MLS and NWSL. -- Philippou

Mark Tatum

Tatum, who previously served as the league's interim president between Lisa Borders' and Engelbert's tenures, would be a surprise pick in some respects. The league has had only female leaders. And, as the longtime deputy commissioner and COO of the NBA, he would be seen as an extension of Silver, putting into question how much autonomy the WNBA really has as a separate entity from the NBA. But if Tatum is seriously considered, it might indicate Silver isn't interested in achieving that dynamic. -- Philippou

ESPN's Ramona Shelburne also contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Arena for 76ers, Flyers to open in 2030, marks 'new era'
stories.summary: The 76ers and Flyers have unveiled renderings of their new fully privately funded arena in South Philadelphia, which is targeted to open before the WNBA season in 2030.
stories.body:
The 76ers and Flyers have unveiled renderings of their new arena on the former Spectrum site in South Philadelphia, which the organizations are calling the largest fully privately funded project in city history.

The arena is now targeted to open before the WNBA season in 2030, when Philadelphia's expansion team will begin play. The Sixers, owned by Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment (HBSE), come in as 50-50 partners with Comcast Spectacor in the new arena, after spending more than a decade as tenants.

"This is a new era for Philadelphia sports," Comcast chairman Brian Roberts said. "To build our future where Ed Snider and the Spectrum made history makes this project truly special. Working with HBSE, we are creating a world-class experience worthy of Philadelphia's incredible fans."

The Spectrum-inspired design includes more than a half-acre of outdoor gathering space, with fan plazas, food and beverage options and a large entrance staircase inspired by the steps at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

"Philly fans deserve the best arena in the world, and we are excited to partner with Comcast to deliver just that," Sixers managing partner Josh Harris said. "This privately funded arena will be the home to moments and memories that define this city for generations."

Added NBA commissioner Adam Silver: "I'm thrilled to see the first renderings of what promises to be an extraordinary home for NBA and WNBA basketball as well as many other world-class events. Beyond the incredible experience the new arena will bring to fans, I commend HBSE and Comcast for such a significant economic investment in Philadelphia."

For the Flyers, the move brings the franchise back to the grounds where it began play in 1967 and won its only two Stanley Cups.

Since taking over as Flyers governor in 2023, Dan Hilferty has also overseen a restructuring of Philadelphia's front office and made returning the franchise to consistent Stanley Cup contention a priority.

"This new arena will be a state-of-the-art home worthy of the Flyers, their fans, and the entire city," NHL commissioner Gary Bettman said. "Comcast Spectacor and HBSE's commitment to this project reflects a shared belief in Philadelphia's future and a lasting investment in the city's economic vitality."

The organizations project the arena will create nearly 15,000 jobs and generate nearly $6 billion in economic activity over the next decade, along with hundreds of millions of dollars in new tax revenue benefiting the city and the School District of Philadelphia.

stories.headline: MLS Power Rankings: Griezmann catapults Orlando into the playoff picture
stories.summary: With eight goal contributions in eight games since joining the Lions, Antoine Griezmann has turned around Orlando's season. That and more in ESPN's MLS Power Rankings.
stories.body:
It's Monday, another weekend of action is in the books, and it's time for the latest edition of ESPN's MLS Power Rankings.

1. Nashville SC
Previous ranking: 1

While Nashville dropped points in a 0-0 draw against New York City on Friday, their biggest competitors for the Supporters' Shield slipped up, too. Both Vancouver and Miami failed to win, leaving Nashville with a 10-point lead atop the Shield race.

2. Vancouver Whitecaps
Previous ranking: 2

Despite taking an early lead, the Whitecaps quickly crumbled in a 3-1 home defeat against St. Louis. In what was, perhaps, their worst match of the season, Vancouver fell apart before halftime en route to losing to fellow contender out West for the second time in four games.

3. St. Louis City SC
Previous ranking: 7

You couldn't have written a better script for St. Louis' Saturday night. Not only did new additions Rafael Navarro and Damion Downs make their debuts in the second half, but the visitors took the game to Vancouver and secured a 3-1 road victory. Doubt St. Louis' contender status at your own peril.

4. Inter Miami CF
Previous ranking: 3

Miami's Achilles heel is widely known: they're a team that gets easily scrambled in their own third. With two sloppy fouls conceding two penalties to Atlanta, Saturday's 2-2 draw with the Five Stripes was the latest example of Inter Miami's defensive play letting them down.

5. LAFC
Previous ranking: 5

Despite holding a one-goal lead heading into the intermission, LAFC's second-half concession saw them earn just a point on the road against Salt Lake. An unwillingness -- or inability -- to keep the ball late in games continues to bite for the Black & Gold.

6. FC Cincinnati
Previous ranking: 6

After their scheduled meeting with D.C. United was postponed due to inclement weather, Cincinnati will have extra time to bed in their defensive reinforcements. That 4-0 loss to Nashville last time out still stings.

7. Chicago Fire
Previous ranking: 4

The good news? Chicago bagged four goals on Saturday, including one from Robert Lewandowski as he continues to find his place in the attack. The bad news? Chicago conceded four in a 4-4 draw with Toronto. It's safe to say Chicago are missing rising star Mbekezeli Mbokazi in the backline.

8. New York City FC
Previous ranking: 9

Up against a fearsome Nashville team, New York City manager Pascal Jansen opted for a fairly conservative approach on Friday. Ceding most of the ball, the Pigeons did well to keep Nashville scoreless, but they failed to create much danger themselves in a 0-0 home draw.

9. New England Revolution
Previous ranking: 8

Trailing by two goals at halftime, the Revs couldn't find a way to equalize against the Galaxy on their way to a 2-1 road defeat. While Carles Gil's penalty conversion got them on the board, questions remain about whether the options New England have placed around him will produce.

10. Houston Dynamo
Previous ranking: 10

Despite having a man advantage for the final 20-plus minutes of the match, Houston had a hard time creating much of anything in their 0-0 road draw with Charlotte. While attacking questions remain for Ben Olsen's outfit, the Dynamo's string of shutdown defensive showings mark them as a team that must be taken seriously.

11. Charlotte FC
Previous ranking: 13

While Charlotte couldn't find a breakthrough during their 0-0 home draw with Houston, Allan Saint-Maximin looked like the best player on the field. Dean Smith's new left winger was at the center of nearly every threatening move and has the look of an MLS star.

12. Real Salt Lake
Previous ranking: 12

Still winless in league play since May, RSL drew 2-2 with LAFC on Saturday. They created a slew of quality chances, but also proved too open in defensive transition as control and tactical balance still eludes them.

13. Orlando City
Previous ranking: 16

Antoine Griezmann continued his absolute tear with the lone goal in Orlando's 1-0 win over San Diego. Now with eight goal contributions in eight games since debuting for the Lions, Griezmann has quickly turned around Orlando's season: they're now above the playoff line in the East.

14. FC Dallas
Previous ranking: 14

If there's a debate about MLS's best striker, Petar Musa is doing his best to end it. The Croatia international managed two goals, including the game winner, and an assist in Dallas' 4-3 win over Kansas City. While the home side's focus lacked, Musa's certainly didn't.

15. Philadelphia Union
Previous ranking: 15

Since league play resumed after the World Cup, the Union are yet to lose. Saturday's 2-0 victory over Montréal lengthened that streak of results to eight games, with six of them going down as wins. With yet another goal from Cavan Sullivan, Philadelphia are flying.

16. San Diego FC
Previous ranking: 15

Missing star midfielder Jeppe Tverskov due to a card suspension, San Diego's ball progression never turned into regular chances in a 1-0 road loss to Orlando. Without the Dane, the sophomore side simply can't carry the same threat going forward.

17. Minnesota United
Previous ranking: 11

For a team that prides itself on effective defending, conceding three goals in the first half in a 5-4 loss to the Timbers was nowhere near good enough for Minnesota. Still, breakout striker Marcus Caldeira's brace could signal longer-term attacking improvement for a team fighting for a playoff spot.

18. LA Galaxy
Previous ranking: 20

The Galaxy marked Sergi Roberto's first MLS start with a 2-1 victory over New England. The former Barcelona man was a touch magnet in central midfield, helping his new team conduct play. If Roberto and Chucky Lozano, who notched an assist, maintain this form, the Galaxy won't be easily dismissed.

19. Toronto FC
Previous ranking: 22

Josh Sargent appears to be finding his form in MLS. While the U.S. striker had a quiet start to life in Toronto, he notched a hat trick in a 4-4 draw with Chicago over the weekend. It was a top-tier showing from Sargent atop Robin Fraser's attacking structure that led to a point for the hosts.

20. Red Bull New York
Previous ranking: 19

Now below the playoff line out East following a 0-0 draw in Seattle, that Red Bull New York didn't do more in the summer transfer window is a major concern. Without any game-changing additions made to the squad before deadline day, it's difficult to see how Michael Bradley's team will rebound.

21. Seattle Sounders
Previous ranking: 21

On Saturday, Sounders fans could breathe a collective sigh of relief upon seeing Cristian Roldan make his first start for the team since May. Still, the USMNT midfielder's return wasn't enough to see Seattle claim their first win in months. A 0-0 draw with the Red Bulls had to suffice.

22. Portland Timbers
Previous ranking: 23

With star striker Kevin Kelsy now off to Rangers in the Scottish Premiership, replacement Vincent Janssen didn't waste any time filling the Venezuelan's shoes. Janssen notched a hat trick in the Timbers' wild 5-4 home win over Minnesota.

23. San Jose Earthquakes
Previous ranking: 18

It looked as if the Quakes' winless run, one that stretches all the way back to May, was going to come to an end on Saturday. That is, until Austin managed a 97th-minute equalizer and a victory turned into a 1-1 draw for San Jose. The Earthquakes are in a bad, bad place.

24. D.C. United
Previous ranking: 24

D.C.'s meeting with Cincinnati was postponed due to weather, leaving the club without a chance to break a five-game winless streak.

25. Austin FC
Previous ranking: 25

Thanks to an equalizer from Guilherme Biro deep in second-half stoppage time, Austin secured a 1-1 draw against San Jose. The result marked four straight games without a loss in league play for the Texas capital club.

26. Columbus Crew
Previous ranking: 27

It didn't take Santi Rodriguez long to open his account in Columbus. The former New York City star bagged the opening goal for the Crew in a 3-0 victory over Colorado. With a remade attack, could this team make a late push for a spot in the postseason?

27. Colorado Rapids
Previous ranking: 26

After trading Navarro to St. Louis and adding new pieces to the attack just before deadline day, the Rapids were nowhere near full strength in a 3-0 loss to the Crew. Colorado will have to wait for their new pieces to arrive and integrate to reach their full potential.

28. Atlanta United
Previous ranking: 28

At last, there are signs of life in Atlanta. During their 2-2 draw with Miami, new striker Breel Embolo made his debut and scored a late equalizer from the spot. Elsewhere, young defensive midfielder Mauricio Amaro made his first MLS appearance and looked extremely comfortable amid his new surroundings.

29. CF Montréal
Previous ranking: 29

Back to the bottom of the East after falling 2-0 in Philadelphia, it's difficult to see Montréal climbing the standings anytime soon. Even with Alexis Sánchez in the lineup, this team is still light on talent.

30. Sporting Kansas City
Previous ranking: 30

Although they managed one of their best attacking outings of the year, spurred on by new winger André Luiz's first start, Kansas City couldn't hold on for a point in Dallas. They fell 4-3 thanks to a late penalty by Musa.

stories.headline: NRL Midweek Mail FW1: Fifita, Latrell feared the worst; Holmes set for World Cup
stories.summary: Blake Lawrie will earn a rare start this weekend before he heads off to join the Super League, while the future of his Dragons teammate Tyrell Sloan is still a little uncertain.
stories.body:
The NRL rarely stands still.

Between training sessions, media appearances, and behind-the-scenes conversations, new storylines often begin to emerge before the weekend arrives.

Throughout the week, ESPN will be gathering notes, insights, and updates from around the competition heading into Week 1 of the NRL finals.

Holmes set for World Cup despite injury

KL Iro has revealed Valentine Holmes is expecting to play for the Cook Islands, despite suffering a syndesmosis injury in the Dragons' last game of the year.

"I saw him yesterday," Iro shared.

"He had a moon boot on, but I think it's a low grade [injury].

"He told me he's sweet to go."

Both stars are expected to suit up for Cook Islands in this year's World Cup

Latrell feared season was over

Latrell Mitchell has revealed there were genuine doubts over whether he would play again this season as he battled the back injury that threatened to derail his finals return.

Mitchell revealed a bulging disc, which he had unknowingly carried for some time, flared during South Sydney's clash with Newcastle and left his return this year in doubt.

"To be fair, I didn't really know if I was gonna play again this year," Mitchell said.

"There were some times there where it definitely was questionable."

The Rabbitohs superstar said the issue became particularly painful during the Newcastle game, despite playing through the second half.

"Apparently I've had it for a very long time," Mitchell said.

"At half-time of the Newcastle Knights game, it was burning me."

Fifita feared career was slipping away
David Fifita has opened up on the "dark days" that left him questioning whether he could return to his destructive best following a string of ankle problems.

The Rabbitohs forward has rediscovered some of his most damaging football heading into the finals, but admitted multiple surgeries across 2024 and 2025 had him second-guessing what his future in the game looked like.

"I had some dark days, second guessing myself and thinking, 'Do I still have it?'" Fifita said.

"I had a few issues with my ankle at the end of 2024 and then... two or three surgeries in that period of time.

"You understand what goes through my head as a 24-year-old. People telling me this and that about my future in the sport."

Fifita said Wayne Bennett's faith has played a major role in rebuilding his confidence since joining South Sydney.

"I've just got a coach that backs me and loves me. I feel the love," he said.

"People thought I was done... and Wayne trusted me, believed in me."

Now preparing for his first finals appearance since 2021, Fifita believes his recent performances have provided the reassurance he needed.

"It reassured me that I still got it."

Finals take on special meaning for Fifita

David Fifita will carry extra motivation into South Sydney's finals campaign, with Friday marking an emotional period for the forward as the first anniversary of his father's death approaches.

Fifita revealed his father tragically passed on September 12 last year, describing the period as an incredibly difficult time for himself and his family.

"It was a very emotional time for my family and myself," Fifita said.

"People don't really know what I went through. To come down here at such a young age and leave all my family... it's very tough."

Fifita had initially planned to return home for the anniversary before South Sydney's finals qualification changed those plans.

"I was supposed to go up there and celebrate the one year, but obviously we're in finals now," he said.

"I'll be doing it for my family and my dad.

"I know my dad is looking [from] above, he's with me every step of the way... I do everything for him."

stories.headline: One thing Deshaun Watson has to improve to remain Browns' starter
stories.summary: Whether the veteran passer can regain dominance over this particular skill will help determine his role in 2026.
stories.body:
When Deshaun Watson takes the field as the Cleveland Browns' starting quarterback during Sunday's Week 1 game (1 p.m. ET, CBS) at the Jacksonville Jaguars, it will likely mark the beginning of his final opportunity to salvage his tenure in Cleveland -- and possibly his NFL career.

Whether Watson can do so hinges on him recapturing a semblance of his Pro Bowl form with the Houston Texans, a player for which the Browns were willing to trade three first-round picks and give a fully-guaranteed $230 million contract in March 2022 after more than two dozen women accused him of sexual assault and inappropriate conduct during massage sessions.

Suspension- and injury-related layoffs have been the story of Watson's time in Cleveland. His latest physical setback is two Achilles surgeries that cost him all of the 2025 season and 22 months between live game action. Watson acknowledged that, at the age of 30 and after multiple significant injuries, his style of play might not resemble that of his peak dual-threat capabilities in Houston.

However, his accuracy on downfield passing and willingness to push the ball -- once a strength -- is an area of his game that has declined in recent years and will need to improve if he wants to keep his job as QB1.

When Watson was named to three consecutive Pro Bowls as a member of the Texans, he wasn't just one of the league's premier mobile quarterbacks but a pinpoint passer able to stretch the field.

In 2018, Watson ranked third among 34 qualifying quarterbacks in completion rate (58.8%) on downfield passes (attempts that traveled at least 10 air yards), according to NFL Next Gen Stats. Watson led the NFL in passing yards in 2020, and he only trailed then-Saints QB Drew Brees in completion rate on downfield pass attempts at 59.9%. Even in Watson's six-game run in his first year in Cleveland after sitting out the 2021 season and serving an 11-game suspension, he completed 53.1% of his downfield passes, which would have ranked sixth.

That mark has declined in recent years. In 2023, Watson completed 39.3% of his downfield attempts, which would have ranked as the worst rate in the league if he qualified. His 33.3% off-target rate on such passes only trailed Panthers QB Bryce Young for the worst in the league. Watson's stat worsened in 2024, as he completed a career-low 37.9% of downfield attempts before his Achilles tear sidelined for the final 10 games of the season.

Compounding Watson's struggles is an aversion to attempting to push the ball downfield. Watson's average depth of target has dropped significantly, from 9 yards in his final Pro Bowl season in 2020 to a career-low 7.1 in his most recent season in 2024, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. Watson threw downfield on a career-low 26.9% of his passes in 2024, his second career season with a rate below 30%, including his 28.8% mark in his 2022 debut season with the Browns.

The struggles coincide with a right, throwing shoulder injury that Watson originally sustained against the Tennessee Titans in Week 3 of the 2023 season. He ultimately underwent season-ending surgery for a fractured glenoid after a Week 10 road win against the Baltimore Ravens.

Watson returned for the start of the 2024 season but never looked comfortable before his season-ending Achilles injury in October 2024.

In his first news conference since rupturing his Achilles, he said in June this was the first time he felt 100% healthy since initially injuring his shoulder against the Titans.

Despite confidence in his physical state, Watson's passing was inconsistent in training camp, and he struggled to push the ball downfield in the preseason. In two preseason games, he was 1 of 6 for 20 yards and an interception on downfield passes; such attempts made up just 22.2% of his passes in the preseason.

"That's something I've always been pretty good at, especially in the past," Watson said Aug. 19. "But those looks and opportunities got to come up. Whatever coach is calling, I try to execute as much as possible, keep the chains moving. Especially early on, it's hard to really start taking shots when the defense is sitting back on that. Especially with Chicago [first preseason game], they were playing a lot of two-wide shells, so a lot of underneath things were right there. But that's something I definitely want to continue to work on, and when those opportunities come, take advantage of it."

Explosive plays are a priority in first-year head coach Todd Monken's offense. In a 2023 presentation at The Harbaugh Academy, Monken listed explosive plays as one of six figures that best explain how teams win games.

After Watson was named the Browns' starting quarterback on Aug. 24 despite struggles in the second preseason game, questions surfaced on how much leeway he would have as QB1. If he's unable to generate the explosive plays Monken desires, Watson's backup, Shedeur Sanders, could provide a more aggressive option.

Though Sanders struggled as a rookie in 2025, his downfield passing -- and willingness to do so -- have been one of his greatest assets. During his seven starts last season, Sanders completed 15 passes on downfield attempts, tied for 19th most among quarterbacks during that span; his 58 downfield attempts were 17th most. Sanders was even better in this year's preseason, completing 5 of 8 of his downfield attempts for 106 yards with a touchdown and an interception (36.4% of his attempts were downfield passes).

Adherence to one of Monken's core tenets could define Watson's 2026 season. Watson's first test comes against a Jaguars defense that allowed a 42.8% completion percentage on downfield throws last season, the fifth-lowest rate in the NFL.

"Everyone's chasing explosives and trying to not to turn it over," Monken said last week. "And that's what you're trying to do. What's the defense trying to do? Turn you over and not allow explosives. That's really the big chess match, is that. The ways that you win.

"Obviously having explosive players helps that. Being able to scheme it up against certain looks and then being able to execute because your protection has to hold up when you get those opportunities. I'm confident in Deshaun and our ability to push the ball down the field, otherwise we wouldn't be starting him."

stories.headline: Kylian Mbappé: Want Champions League win 'more than anything,' more important than Ballon d'Or
stories.summary: Kylian Mbappé said he wants to win the Champions League "more than anything" -- and that he'd prefer it to winning the Ballon d'Or -- after Real Madrid's 2-1 win over Inter on Tuesday.
stories.body:
Kylian Mbappé said he wants to win the Champions League "more than anything" -- and that he'd prefer it to winning the Ballon d'Or -- after Real Madrid's 2-1 win over Inter on Tuesday.

Mbappé and Federico Valverde put Madrid 2-0 up in the first half at the Bernabéu, taking advantage of two defensive mistakes from Inter, before Carlos Augusto pulled a goal back for the visitors in the second half.

Inter dominated the game for long periods, but Madrid took all three points in José Mourinho's first European game back at the club.

"That's the objective, that's the goal," Mbappé told CBS, when asked about lifting the Champions League this season. "That's what I said yesterday about the Ballon d'Or, but the Champions League is even more important. I play for the club of my dreams.

"It's really important for me to win the Champions League here in Madrid, I want it more than anything. But of course the Ballon d'Or this year, I think it's a great opportunity. It's a good year for me."

Mbappé has been nominated for the men's Ballon d'Or after scoring 10 goals at the World Cup this summer as France reached the semifinals.

However he has failed to win a major trophy with his club since arriving at Madrid two years ago.

Last season, Madrid were eliminated by Bayern Munich in the quarterfinals.

"It's really early," he said, when asked about the team's prospects. "We just started the Champions League now, we started with a win. But of course we want to do special things.

"We want to be a collective, we want to be a team who can compete with all the best teams in the world. We know that last year was a bit difficult for us in the Champions League.

"At Real Madrid you always have to be at the top, I hope this year we'll compete as a collective, to be where we want to be."
